To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
voltage-dependent anion channels are present in the plasma membranes of guard cells.

voltage-dependent anion channels exist in the plasma membrane (plasmalema) of guard cells and that these channels have a conductive capacity of 39 picosiemens and are permeable to chloride and malate ions.
Voltage-dependent anion channels provide an anion pathway that is required for the release of chloride and malate from guard cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the mechanisms that regulate stomatal opening and closure.
the molecular mechanisms of the regulation of gas exchange in plants.
the molecular mechanisms of stomatal movements, which are essential for the gas exchange of plants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the guard cell plasma membrane contains a voltage-dependent anion channel which is permeable to chloride and malate, and which is active at membrane potentials above −80 mV.

the guard cell plasma membrane is endowed with a voltage–dependent anionic channel, which is permeable to chloride and malate and which is responsible for the anionic component of the efflux of solutes from guard cells during stomatal closure.
voltage-dependent anion channels are involved in the regulation of the turgor-driven movement of guard cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
voltage-dependent anion channels are the missing link between K+ channels and the turgor-operating mechanism in guard cells.
the anion channels in guard cell plasmalemma are the missing link in the mechanism of stomatal closure.
voltage-dependent anion channels provide the anionic counterpart to voltage-dependent K+ channels in the regulation of guard cell turgor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we identified voltage-dependent anion channels (VDAC) in the plasmalemma of guard cells.
we identified the anion channel responsible for the release of anions from guard cells, which are essential for the closing of stomatal pores in plants.

we identified voltage-dependent anion channels that are active in the guard cell plasma membrane, and we showed that the channels are permeable to chloride and malate and are involved in the regulation of stomatal aperture.
